Both flow readers describe the declared grouping-by-part order (reading vocabulary, Parts I-VIII as a chain, Veldmark last, index at the end) and mark every section's position clear. Not recorded as failures, as non-material or outside the prose units (row contents, which the spec does not govern): forward references inside rows (Trader traceability and Part V rows leaning on the DSA row, reported by A3 and B3; A said it did not need to re-read), tenant and entitlements used in rows before their own rows (B4, B5), External vs Listing system of record far apart (B7), Material change row (A3), Veldmark row order (A6), the awkward Part VIII bridge (A4, 'not confusing'), and the layout given twice in p01 and p02 (B8, 'did not get lost'; the spec's roadmap places it so).

results.draft_locus: Reading the Book: Evidence Labels and Failure Patterns ¶1
results.finding: The fifteen failure-pattern rows follow neither the parts nor the alphabet: the first ten roughly follow the parts, then Vanity Liquidity (Part I), Billing by Guesswork (Part VI) and Set-and-Forget AI (Part VII) come last, and the lead paragraph does not say what order they are in. The section's grouping is sound; p04 should state the order (e.g. as in where-listing-systems-go-wrong) or the rows should be sorted by repairing part.
results.quote: For each pattern, the last column below links to [[where-listing-systems-go-wrong]] and to the chapter that does most of the repair work.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B item 2 (Reading the Book: 'the order of the fifteen failure patterns inside it is unclear: not alphabetical, not by part'); flow-A item A1

results.finding: Both flow readers had to re-read the Part III lead's last clause, which defines lead ledger and lead management by forward reference to a term defined three sections later. The order is the spec's (Part III before Part VI) and the pointer is required; the long, back-loaded sentence obscures it. A shorter, separate pointer sentence would remove the re-read.
results.quote: [[professional-seller-tooling]] owns what professionals use, including the lead ledger and lead management, the professional's side of the lead that Part VI defines.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B item B2 (same sentence, 'Had to re-read'); flow-A item A2

results.corroborated_by: flow-B item B9; flow-A item A5

results.finding: The index entries 'Instance attribute (aspect)' and 'Product attribute (aspect)' carry an alias 'aspect' that does not appear in the Part II rows they link to, so the reader cannot confirm the alias where it lands.

The opening example uses contact, conversation and lead, and Part I rows use 'contact' heavily, but the three are defined only in Part VI, about 300 lines down, with no pointer. The difficulty comes from the declared grouping by part (spec flow), which the spec accepts; a pointer to Part VI in p01 or the Part I lead would ease it.
results.quote: a buyer's first chat message to a dealer is a contact, opens a conversation and may create a lead, and a report that adds the three together counts nothing useful.

results.finding: The Veldmark lead says the earlier terms describe real practice, but earlier rows carry Veldmark specifics (Migration stage gate 'Veldmark uses five per slice'; Marketplace fitness function 'Veldmark's scorecard has twelve'), and p03 itself says Veldmark is named in some rows. The contrast should be between real terms and fictional names, not imply earlier rows are free of Veldmark.
results.quote: The terms so far describe real marketplace practice; this last section is different.

results.finding: Terms in the prose units are either on already_knows (APIs, event streams, Veldmark as fictional group, toolkit templates) or defined on the page: the does_not_know items (near-synonyms, owning chapters, other verticals' terms) are all given in rows with owning chapters. 'Reading vocabulary' in p01 is unpacked by p02 at once. Undefined 'qualified contact' (AC-1 reader) and tenant/entitlement before their rows (B4, B5) are row contents, which this spec does not govern, and are defined or common to this audience; no flow reader reported a prose-unit term as unexplained.
p01 opens with the page's function and a concrete example (the buyer's first message counted three ways), not a placeholder, restated question, dictionary definition, sweeping history or book report.

p15 does not open with 'in conclusion', adds no new subtopic or body evidence and does more than restate the thesis: it turns the rule into a course of action. p16 is a hand-off pointer, as the spec declares.

'Read together, the sections and this index give every term in the book one meaning and one owning chapter' is stated by no single section; the so-what follows: 'Before a term goes into a metric definition, a contract or a policy, look it up here...'.

The callback returns to the hook, but names it as 'the dealer's first message', which reverses the sender: the hook is a buyer's first chat message to a dealer. The AC-1 cold reader was briefly confused by the reversal. The spec's synthesis and p15 controlling idea share the loose wording, but callback.to and the hook make the buyer the sender; 'the buyer's first message to the dealer' fixes it.
results.quote: so the dealer's first message can be counted as a contact, a conversation or a lead on purpose, never by accident.

results.finding: The intro-only reader predicts the order: how-to-use section, reading vocabulary, one section per part, Veldmark names, alphabetical index; all four roadmap promises are kept in that order. Its uncertainties ('reading vocabulary', how many parts) are resolved by s-how, which the roadmap names as the full map.

The reader gives the organization (reading vocabulary, a section per part, Veldmark names, index at the end) and the use (look up, read neighbors for contrasts, follow the owning-chapter link, one meaning per term, a disagreement means one is wrong and the chapter's worked example decides, check regulatory/company terms as of 2026 before use), matching expected.
